Wall Street: the Dow Jones climbs back above 50,000 points, but Nvidia falls 6% again and markets put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 98%

On Tuesday, November 24, the New York Stock Exchange split in two. The Dow Jones rose 0.85% and closed above 50,000 points, but the Nasdaq lost 1.48%: Nvidia gave back about 6%, a day after a 31.5% jump, and Anthropic fell below its IPO price [3][4].
The Dow Jones, which tracks 30 large US companies, rose 0.85% to 50,018.70 points. The S&P 500 lost 0.50% to 7,201.09 points, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 1.48% to 23,733.54 points [4].
For the S&P 500, it was the eighth decline in nine sessions [1]. The day before, the Nasdaq had jumped nearly 7% [3].
Nvidia lost about 6%. On Monday, the stock had climbed 31.5% after Jensen Huang returned to lead the company, under pressure from Donald Trump [3].

Anthropic, which went public a few days ago, closed below its IPO price of $83, down 6.5% according to Reuters; during the session, it had fallen 11% [1][5]. Hewlett Packard Enterprise plunged 16%, while healthcare stocks gained 2.9% [5].
Yet American households are regaining confidence: the Conference Board index rose from 91.9 in October to 103.3 in November, well above the expected 92.5 [1].
The dollar fell 0.44% against major currencies, after hitting its highest level in 20 months [3]. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury slipped from 4.92% to 4.90% [1].
Investors put the probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December at about 98% [3].
Key takeaway: Monday's spectacular rebound did not hold, and money is leaving artificial intelligence stocks for sectors seen as safer, such as healthcare and traditional industry [3][5].

The fear is still the same: that AI stocks have risen too high and will end up deflating like a bubble [1]. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer of UBS Global Wealth Management, says this pullback does not yet prove that the underlying trend in AI investment is broken [5]. For Tom Hulick, of Strategy Asset Managers, Jensen Huang remains “for now” the right person to lead Nvidia [2].

The other issue is inflation. At the end of October, the first estimate put US growth at an annualized 3.4% in the third quarter, above expectations, and the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 3.6% year on year in September [6][7]. Such a strong economy pushes the Fed to raise rates rather than cut them.
The October PCE figure, released on Wednesday, November 25, the day before Thanksgiving, will therefore be decisive ahead of the December meeting [3].

If the Fed raises rates in December, the dollar is likely to stay expensive: your purchases in dollars and oil, which is paid for in dollars, will cost more. And if you have an index fund or a stock savings plan with US shares, expect more sharp swings, especially in AI stocks.

Hormuz: Iran vows to close the strait “a little more every day” and rejects any talks without its seven conditions, as Washington targets its “shadow bank”

On Tuesday, November 24, Iran's army chief, General Amir Hatami, ordered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to be tightened every day until Washington accepts seven conditions. The United States sanctioned some thirty targets in Iran's parallel financial system. Brent rebounded by $2.03, to $91.40 [1][2][4][6].

Major General Amir Hatami, head of the Iranian army, said the strait would not reopen until Tehran's seven conditions are met, and ordered the navy to close it “a little more every day” [1]. He warned that a new US war would bring harsher strikes [1].
The speaker of Parliament and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said there would be “neither action nor negotiation” until these conditions are applied [2].

These conditions have never been officially published. According to Iranian state media, they include lifting sanctions, ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and returning seized Iranian assets [2].

According to Iran, only two ships crossed the strait in 24 hours and 400 are waiting to pass [7]. The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported three ships hit by unidentified projectiles while heading east; all continued on their way, with no casualties among the crews [6].

The US Treasury sanctioned 22 companies and 8 individuals, including exchange houses and the Iranian Center for Currency and Gold Exchange, which connects Iranian exporters and importers [4][5]. Washington is also investigating Iran's role in cyberattacks against some fifty ships [3].

According to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Treasury's anti-money-laundering office, about $14.7 billion in transactions between January 2025 and August 2026 may be linked to this parallel system, more than half of it going to the United Arab Emirates [5].
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Iran's economy is “underwater” and its leaders are “panicking” [8]. Qatar's prime minister, for his part, urged Marco Rubio and JD Vance to restart talks [1].

Key takeaway: both sides are hardening their positions at the same time. Tehran sets preconditions for any dialogue, Washington tightens the financial squeeze further, and the Qatari mediator has achieved nothing so far [1][2][4].

The “shadow bank” is the network that lets Iran sell its oil and import goods despite sanctions: exchange houses and shell companies, often in the Emirates, settle payments outside the official banking system [5]. The Treasury threatens to cut off from the US financial system any entity that helps Iran evade sanctions [5].

Oil nevertheless remains under control. Brent had fallen during the day to its lowest level since August before rising again, because the International Energy Agency expects a global surplus from late 2026, even larger in 2027 [6].

As long as the global oil surplus holds, the Hormuz blockade has little effect on what you pay to fill up. But a strait closed “a little more every day”, with no talks in sight, leaves prices at the mercy of an incident: a tanker actually sunk could push up gasoline and heating costs within days.

2027 budget: Brussels gives France the green light, but forecasts a 5.4% deficit, not 5% as Paris does

On Tuesday, November 24, the European Commission found France's draft budget for 2027 compliant with EU rules, because spending stays below the set ceiling. But it forecasts a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2027, above the government's 5% target, and warns that everything depends on Parliament [1][2][3].
The opinion is part of the “autumn package” of the European Semester, the annual review of eurozone countries' budgets, published on Tuesday, November 24 [3][4].

Brussels no longer judges only the deficit, but the growth in net public spending (excluding interest on debt and certain other items). It forecasts this at 1.1% in 2027, below the 1.2% ceiling set by the EU Council [4][5].

The government is targeting a deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027, after 5.4% in 2026 and 5.1% in 2025. The Commission, for its part, forecasts 5.5% this year and 5.4% next year, far from the European limit of 3% [1][2].
Its forecasts published on November 17 also differ on the economy: 0.6% growth in 2027, against 1% in the French budget, and 2.9% inflation, against 1.9% [5].

Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis is not calling for stricter spending control “for now” [3]. But he warns: “If there are problems with the budget, or significant deviations, this could lead to a reassessment of the situation” [3].
The Commission highlights “considerable uncertainty” linked to the ongoing debates in Parliament, where the government has no majority [1].
Key takeaway: Brussels is not penalizing France, but this reprieve rests on a budget that has not yet been passed and on forecasts more optimistic than its own [1][3][5].

France remains under the excessive deficit procedure: it has until 2029 to get back below 3% [1][6]. Along with Belgium, it has the largest deficit in the eurozone [1]. According to the draft budget, public debt is set to rise further to 121.7% of GDP in 2027 [7]. ING economists note that, even if fully implemented, this budget would only slow the rise in debt [8].

In the Senate, the review of the “revenue” part of the state budget, which has received more than 3,000 amendments, is expected to last until November 28 or 29 [9]. Economy Minister Roland Lescure is defending an effort of €54 billion in 2027 there, and has already mentioned Article 49.3, which allows a bill to be adopted without a vote [10].
If the final text strays too far from the version approved, Brussels could revise its judgment in the spring [3][5].

This green light spares France a new warning that could have pushed up the rates at which the state borrows, and therefore, eventually, those on your mortgage. But it settles nothing: the €54 billion in savings and tax increases still has to be voted on, and it will affect your tax bill or your public services.

EU–Balkans summit in Brussels: Serbia, without a government, stays away, while Montenegro still aims to join by 2028

Leaders of the EU and the Western Balkans meet this Wednesday, November 25, in Brussels, with António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. Serbia, still trying to form a government after its elections, announced it would not attend, and Kosovo's presence had not been confirmed [1][2][3][4].
The EU is represented by European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen [1][2].
On the agenda: the reforms needed to join the EU, progress on the “Growth Plan” for the Western Balkans and the region's security [2][3].

Serbia's acting president, Aleksandar Čupić, announced that his country would not take part in the summit, according to Table.Briefings [4]. The EU's 27 members expect the new team in Belgrade to normalize relations with Kosovo and impose sanctions on Russia [4].
For Kosovo, the name of its representative had not yet been announced on the eve of the summit [3].
In June 2026, at the previous summit in Tivat, Montenegro, Ursula von der Leyen declared: “Montenegro, the 28th member state by 2028, is within reach. We hope Albania will follow quickly” [5].

The Tivat summit was attended by Serbia's then president, Aleksandar Vučić, who came despite the opposing advice of his intelligence services [6]. In December 2025, in Brussels, he had boycotted the meeting [7].
Key takeaway: the EU wants to keep up the pace of enlargement in the Balkans, but Serbia's empty chair, for the second time in a year, shows the limits of the exercise [4][7].

The race is between two countries. In December 2025, António Costa said Montenegro's path had “clearly accelerated” and that Albania had opened all its negotiating chapters “in a very short time” [8]. According to the Commission, Montenegro can wrap up its negotiations by the end of 2026 if it keeps this pace, and Albania by the end of 2027 [9].
The “Growth Plan”, adopted at the December 2024 summit, should according to the EU double the region's economic growth within ten years [10]. It ties European money to reforms.

Kosovo remains a case apart: the summit date had been known since October, but Pristina's presence was still not confirmed [2][3]. For Belgrade, normalizing relations with Kosovo remains one of the conditions set by the Europeans [4].

A 28th member means a slightly larger single market, but also European money, and so partly yours through the EU budget, paid to these countries to fund their reforms. And the stability of the Balkans, on the EU's doorstep, matters for the security of all of Europe.

news.2026-11-25-japon-cpi-contribution-a: Japan: facing Trump's sanctions, Takaichi will pay its 2027 share to the International Criminal Court this year

Receiving the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Japan's Tomoko Akane, in Tokyo on Tuesday, November 24, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to pay Japan's entire 2027 contribution before the end of 2026, as Washington sanctions the Court [1][2][3][4].
Tokyo usually pays its share in April or later [1].
Japan is the ICC's largest contributor, ahead of Germany, France and the United Kingdom: 4.6 billion yen ($28.8 million) in 2026, nearly 15% of the annual budget [1].
The United States sanctioned Judge Akane in August, then the Court itself on October 9: Americans are no longer allowed to provide it with money, goods or services without a Treasury license [2].
It was the first meeting between the two women since January [3].
Key takeaway: a very close ally of Washington, Tokyo is choosing to help an institution that the Trump administration wants to starve [1][2].

The sanctions are due to take full effect in April 2027 and could disrupt the Court's banking and IT operations; the money will be used to “ensure its survival” and pay salaries, Tomoko Akane said [2].
France is among the ICC's biggest funders [1]: if the Court falters, the international justice for war crimes that Paris champions loses ground.

news.2026-11-25-suede-kristersson-vote-3: Sweden: still without a government after 72 days, Ulf Kristersson tries his luck on Monday, ahead of a possible new election

The speaker of the Swedish Parliament, Andreas Norlén, announced on Tuesday, November 24, a vote on Monday, November 30, at 1 p.m., on conservative Ulf Kristersson as prime minister, after 72 days of negotiations since the general election [1][2].
“I have decided to propose Ulf Kristersson as candidate for prime minister,” Andreas Norlén said [1].
It will be the third vote on a prime minister: the candidate is rejected only if at least 175 of the 349 members vote against [2].

Ulf Kristersson wants to govern with the Moderates, the Centre Party, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, but the Centre Party has not agreed to join the government; it has only promised to broaden the talks [2].
Key takeaway: Sweden has only two attempts left to avoid a return to the polls [1][2].
If Monday fails, a fourth and final vote will take place before Christmas; if that fails too, a snap election must be held within three months [1][2].
An EU country without a fully empowered government carries less weight in European decisions, on Ukraine as well as on the common budget: a new election would delay that return even further.
